clinicalPearls: One of the smallest human intestinal flukes, acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish carrying metacercariae, particularly in East Asia
Light infection is usually asymptomatic; heavier burdens cause colicky abdominal pain, intermittent diarrhoea, nausea and lethargy
Adult flukes attach to the mucosa of the small intestine and provoke local inflammation and mild malabsorption
Diagnosis relies on finding small operculated eggs in stool that closely resemble those of Opisthorchis, Clonorchis and other heterophyids
Rarely, eggs or flukes enter the circulation and embolise to the heart or brain, causing ectopic disease
Praziquantel is highly effective and the treatment of choice
Prevention centres on avoiding raw freshwater fish and improving sanitation to reduce egg contamination
reference.pathophysiology: Metagonimus yokogawai is a minute intestinal trematode whose life cycle passes through freshwater snails and then freshwater fish, in which infective metacercariae encyst. Humans and other fish-eating animals acquire infection by consuming raw or undercooked fish. The larvae excyst in the small intestine and mature into tiny adult flukes that burrow among the villi of the jejunum, causing localised mucosal inflammation, villous flattening and superficial ulceration. Heavy infection can impair absorption and produce chronic diarrhoea. Occasionally eggs deposited in the mucosa penetrate vessels and are carried to distant organs such as the myocardium or central nervous system, where they excite a granulomatous reaction. Eggs excreted in faeces continue the cycle by contaminating freshwater.
additionalDifferentials: Heterophyiasis and other heterophyid intestinal fluke infection
Fasciolopsiasis and other intestinal trematode disease
Opisthorchiasis or clonorchiasis (from egg morphology overlap)
Irritable bowel syndrome or functional dyspepsia
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites with concentration techniques
Repeated stool examination given intermittent and low egg output
Careful egg morphometry to distinguish from other small trematode eggs
Imaging or echocardiography only if ectopic (cardiac or cerebral) disease is suspected
Serology where available to support the diagnosis
redFlags: Neurological deficit or seizures suggesting cerebral egg embolisation
Cardiac symptoms raising concern for myocardial involvement
Persistent diarrhoea with weight loss and evidence of malabsorption
Failure to respond to treatment, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent for intestinal disease, which resolves promptly with anthelmintic therapy; the rare ectopic cardiac or cerebral forms can be serious depending on the site affected.
pitfalls: Misidentifying the eggs as those of opisthorchiid liver flukes because of near-identical morphology
Overlooking light infections when only a single stool sample is examined
Attributing non-specific gastrointestinal symptoms to functional disease in endemic settings
Failing to consider ectopic embolisation when unexplained cardiac or neurological signs appear
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat with the anthelmintic praziquantel, which is highly effective and the agent of choice for intestinal fluke infection
Provide supportive rehydration and correct any malabsorption or nutritional deficit from heavy infection
Confirm cure with follow-up stool microscopy, allowing for intermittent low egg output
Treat household members and others who shared the same raw or undercooked freshwater fish source
Manage rare ectopic cardiac or cerebral disease with anthelmintic therapy plus organ-specific supportive or surgical care and relevant specialist referral
Advise on prevention through thorough cooking of freshwater fish and avoidance of raw preparations
